issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma, 'Similar cars' is hard to justify as a salient trigger unless the disaster specifically involved a vehicle context, which is not suggested anywhere else in the profile. The other triggers ('feeling physically unwell', 'unpredictable situations') and the negative appraisals describe generalized vulnerability and loss of control, but 'similar cars' introduces a highly specific cue that does not cohere with the rest of the formulation or trauma type.

For a natural disaster trauma, 'Alcohol smell' is a hard-to-explain trigger unless supported by memory or threat content linking alcohol odor to the disaster context. Here there are no Memory or Threat items providing that connection, making this trigger clinically incoherent with the trauma type and the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
issues.explanation: The formulation shows a strong Triggers → Negative Appraisals link, but the selected trigger items mostly imply internal-state or unpredictability cues, whereas 'I have to be on guard all the time' implies an ongoing external danger/threat style response. With Threat node absent and no trigger content clearly tied to vigilance for danger, this appraisal is weakly matched to the trigger pattern and stands out as formulation-incongruent in this profile.

vignette: Mr. Nguyen is a 51-year-old South Eastern Asian man who works as a policy analyst and has been married for over two decades. His life changed drastically after he experienced a severe natural disaster—a powerful tornado—that tore through his community last year. During the tornado, Mr. Nguyen found himself trapped in a building with broken windows and debris swirling around him. The smell of burning wood and smoke was overwhelming as fires broke out nearby. He felt physically ill from the fear and helplessness, and the unpredictability of the situation only heightened his anxiety. Since then, any feeling of being unwell or exposure to unpredictable situations triggers intense distress and flashbacks for Mr. Nguyen. Mr. Nguyen has come to believe that he can't rely on himself in such situations anymore. His experience during the tornado made him feel utterly vulnerable, and now he is certain that if something goes wrong again, he won’t be able to protect himself or his family. This belief exacerbates his fear of going crazy. He constantly worries about how his heightened reactions might indicate a deeper mental health issue. The thought of losing control in an unpredictable situation terrifies him. This constant vigilance has taken a toll on Mr. Nguyen’s daily life and work. At the office, he avoids attending meetings that might run late or involve unexpected turns, as any unpredictability makes him feel physically ill. Recently, his fear of being unwell led to a significant decrease in productivity, as he would leave early if even a slight feeling of nausea arose. His colleagues have noticed changes in his behavior, but Mr. Nguyen is too afraid to address it directly. At home, the smell of smoke during a cooking mishap can send him into a panic. He has become hypervigilant about any potential fire hazards and insists on checking all appliances repeatedly, which strains his relationship with his wife. She notices that he seems on edge most of the time but is unsure how to help. The unpredictability of everyday life now feels unbearable for Mr. Nguyen. Even small changes in routine can trigger a cascade of anxiety and fear. He had come to believe that these reactions mean he’s going crazy, which further intensifies his negative appraisals about himself. This vicious cycle has led him to become increasingly isolated, both at work and at home. What finally prompted Mr. Nguyen to seek help was an incident where he left a crucial meeting early due to feeling ill. His supervisor noticed the pattern of absenteeism and suggested professional support. Now, as he considers therapy, what frightens him most is the prospect that his fears might indeed be justified—that he won’t be able to function normally again without significant intervention. On the other hand, he hopes that understanding these reactions will provide some relief from the overwhelming anxiety that has come to dominate his life. Mr. Nguyen’s journey since the tornado illustrates a profound shift in how he perceives himself and the world around him. The traumatic event has left deep marks on his psyche, making even minor triggers potent reminders of his vulnerability. His fear of unpredictability and physical illness now fuel each other in a self-reinforcing cycle that he hopes to break through therapy.
